difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that antibiotic resistance is a serious problem; disagreement hinges on a specific causal axis (agricultural vs. clinical use) rather than a total contradiction. One trap answer captures their shared concern.
stimulus: Moreno: The overuse of antibiotics in livestock farming is the primary driver of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Farmers administer these drugs not just to treat illness but to accelerate growth, exposing entire herds to antibiotics and creating ideal conditions for resistance to evolve. Reducing agricultural antibiotic use would therefore do more to protect public health than any clinic-based intervention. Peña: Antibiotic resistance is indeed a grave threat, but the main culprit is the inappropriate prescribing of antibiotics by physicians. Patients demand prescriptions for viral infections, and many doctors comply. Agricultural reform is worthwhile, but curbing clinical overprescription would yield the greatest public health gains.
questionStem: Moreno and Peña disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: antibiotic resistance poses a serious threat to public health

choices.label: B
choices.text: reducing antibiotic use in agriculture would have any public health benefit

choices.label: C
choices.text: the primary source of antibiotic resistance is the agricultural rather than the clinical sector

choices.label: D
choices.text: physicians are capable of correctly diagnosing viral infections

choices.label: E
choices.text: antibiotic-resistant bacteria can be transmitted from livestock to humans

explanations.correct: Moreno explicitly argues agricultural overuse is the primary driver; Peña explicitly argues inappropriate clinical prescribing is the main culprit. Both directly take opposing positions on which sector is the primary source.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers acknowledge antibiotic resistance is a serious threat.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — Peña calls agricultural reform 'worthwhile,' so both actually agree it has some benefit. Only one speaker denies primacy, not all benefit.
explanations.D: One-sided — neither speaker directly addresses physicians' diagnostic accuracy; Peña mentions patient demand and physician compliance, not diagnostic skill.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses the transmission mechanism from livestock to humans.

difficultyReason: Both speakers share common ground on carbon pricing in principle; their disagreement is about which mechanism — tax or cap-and-trade — is superior in practice. A trap answer exploits their shared endorsement of carbon pricing.
stimulus: Nakamura: A carbon tax is the most effective tool for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. It sets a clear price signal that businesses can plan around, and revenues can be returned to citizens as dividends, making the policy politically durable. Cap-and-trade schemes, by contrast, are vulnerable to price volatility and political manipulation of permit allocations. Osei: Carbon taxes sound appealing in theory, but cap-and-trade systems are superior in practice. By setting a firm emissions ceiling, cap-and-trade guarantees a specific environmental outcome regardless of how firms respond. A carbon tax only changes incentives — it cannot ensure that actual emissions will fall to any particular level.
questionStem: Nakamura and Osei disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: placing a price on carbon emissions is an appropriate policy response to climate change

choices.label: B
choices.text: carbon taxes provide businesses with a predictable price signal

choices.label: C
choices.text: cap-and-trade systems are more effective than carbon taxes at reducing greenhouse gas emissions

choices.label: D
choices.text: governments should return carbon tax revenues to citizens

choices.label: E
choices.text: greenhouse gas emissions are the leading cause of climate change

explanations.correct: Nakamura argues the carbon tax is the most effective tool and criticizes cap-and-trade; Osei argues cap-and-trade is superior in practice. This is the direct axis of disagreement.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers endorse carbon pricing as an appropriate response; they only disagree about which mechanism is better.
explanations.B: One-sided — Nakamura affirms this, but Osei does not address the predictability of the price signal; Osei's critique concerns outcome certainty, not price predictability.
explanations.D: One-sided — Nakamura mentions revenue dividends; Osei never addresses what should be done with tax revenues.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses the causal relationship between emissions and climate change.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that the jury system has value; disagreement centers on whether professional judges would deliver more accurate verdicts. A trap answer captures their shared premise about the importance of accurate verdicts.
stimulus: Hartley: The jury system, while democratic in spirit, frequently produces inaccurate verdicts. Jurors lack legal training, are susceptible to emotional appeals, and often misunderstand complex evidence. Replacing jury trials with panels of professional judges in serious criminal cases would yield more reliable outcomes and better serve justice. Drummond: Professional judges are not infallible, and their decisions can reflect institutional biases acquired over years on the bench. Juries bring diverse perspectives that help guard against such bias. The occasional inaccuracy that comes with lay judgment is an acceptable price for verdicts that reflect community values rather than professional insularity.
questionStem: Hartley and Drummond disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: accurate verdicts are an important goal of a criminal justice system

choices.label: B
choices.text: professional judges are entirely free from bias in their decision-making

choices.label: C
choices.text: juries are susceptible to emotional appeals during trials

choices.label: D
choices.text: replacing juries with professional judges would produce more accurate verdicts in serious criminal cases

choices.label: E
choices.text: the jury system should be abolished in all civil as well as criminal proceedings

explanations.correct: Hartley explicitly argues professional judges would yield more reliable outcomes; Drummond argues judges carry institutional biases and that lay judgment, despite occasional inaccuracy, is preferable. They directly oppose each other on whether switching to judges improves accuracy.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers treat accurate verdicts as an important goal; they disagree about how best to achieve them.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — Hartley does not claim judges are entirely bias-free; Hartley only claims they are more reliable than juries. The proposition in (B) is stronger than Hartley's actual claim.
explanations.C: One-sided — Hartley asserts this; Drummond does not directly contest whether juries are susceptible to emotional appeals.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses civil proceedings; Hartley limits the proposal to serious criminal cases.

difficultyReason: Both speakers value preserving endangered languages; they disagree on whether immersive school programs are the most effective preservation method. A trap presents their shared concern about language loss as a disagreement.
stimulus: Vasquez: Endangered languages are best preserved through immersive school programs that teach children entirely in the heritage language. Schools create a new generation of fluent speakers, and fluency — not just cultural memory — is what keeps a language alive. Community events and digital archives, while helpful, are supplementary at best. Lindqvist: Immersive schooling can actually alienate families if parents themselves are not fluent, creating a divide between home and classroom. The most effective preservation happens when communities integrate the language into daily life — through markets, local governance, and inter-generational conversation. Schools matter, but they are not the primary engine of revitalization.
questionStem: Vasquez and Lindqvist disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the preservation of endangered languages is a worthwhile social goal

choices.label: B
choices.text: digital archives have any role to play in language preservation

choices.label: C
choices.text: immersive school programs are the most effective means of preserving endangered languages

choices.label: D
choices.text: children must achieve full fluency for a language to survive

choices.label: E
choices.text: governments should fund endangered language programs

explanations.correct: Vasquez argues immersive school programs are the best preservation tool; Lindqvist argues community integration into daily life is more effective and that schools are not the primary engine. Both take clear opposing positions.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers clearly treat language preservation as worthwhile; neither questions its value.
explanations.B: One-sided — Vasquez calls digital archives supplementary; Lindqvist does not address digital archives at all.
explanations.D: One-sided — Vasquez implicitly endorses full fluency as the goal; Lindqvist's position concerns where language integration occurs, not whether fluency is needed.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses government funding.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that the gig economy has changed labor markets; they share the view that workers deserve protections. Disagreement lies in whether classifying gig workers as employees is the right mechanism for delivering those protections.
stimulus: Chandra: Gig workers — drivers, delivery couriers, freelance taskers — deserve the same protections as traditional employees: minimum wage guarantees, access to unemployment insurance, and employer contributions to health benefits. The only way to achieve this is to reclassify them as employees. Their nominal independence is a legal fiction that benefits corporations at workers' expense. Bellamy: Gig workers genuinely value the flexibility that comes with independent contractor status, and mandatory reclassification would destroy that. Worker protections should instead be extended through portable benefits legislation — policies that attach benefits to individuals rather than to employment relationships. Reclassification is neither necessary nor desirable for protecting these workers.
questionStem: Chandra and Bellamy disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: gig workers are entitled to some form of labor protections

choices.label: B
choices.text: reclassifying gig workers as employees is the appropriate means of securing their labor protections

choices.label: C
choices.text: many gig workers prefer flexible working arrangements to fixed schedules

choices.label: D
choices.text: corporations benefit financially from the independent contractor classification

choices.label: E
choices.text: portable benefits legislation has been successfully implemented in any jurisdiction

explanations.correct: Chandra says reclassification is the only way to achieve worker protections; Bellamy says reclassification is neither necessary nor desirable, preferring portable benefits instead. Both directly address and oppose each other on this mechanism.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers agree gig workers deserve protections; the dispute is over method, not entitlement.
explanations.C: One-sided — Bellamy asserts workers value flexibility; Chandra calls their independence a 'legal fiction' but does not directly address whether workers subjectively prefer it.
explanations.D: One-sided — Chandra asserts this; Bellamy does not dispute or address it.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker discusses the historical track record of portable benefits laws.

difficultyReason: Both speakers share concern about social media's effects on democratic discourse; they diverge on whether algorithmic content ranking is the cause. A trap answer presents their shared worry as a point of contention.
stimulus: Eriksson: Social media platforms' algorithmic ranking systems are the root cause of political polarization online. By prioritizing emotionally provocative content, these algorithms drive users into ideological echo chambers, eroding the shared factual foundation that democratic deliberation requires. Regulating algorithmic design should therefore be a top legislative priority. Walcott: Political polarization predates social media and would persist without it. Research shows that most people encounter more cross-cutting political content online than they do in their offline social circles. The algorithms are not the villain — pre-existing partisan identities drive users to select polarizing content regardless of how feeds are ranked.
questionStem: Eriksson and Walcott disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: political polarization is a threat to democratic deliberation

choices.label: B
choices.text: social media platforms use algorithms to rank the content users see

choices.label: C
choices.text: social media algorithms are a primary cause of political polarization

choices.label: D
choices.text: legislatures have the authority to regulate the design of social media algorithms

choices.label: E
choices.text: users encounter any politically diverse content through social media feeds

explanations.correct: Eriksson asserts algorithms are the root cause of polarization; Walcott argues polarization predates social media and that pre-existing partisan identities, not algorithms, drive polarizing content consumption. They directly oppose each other on this causal claim.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both treat polarization as a problem; Eriksson explicitly and Walcott implicitly treat it as something to be concerned about.
explanations.B: One-sided — Eriksson discusses algorithmic ranking; Walcott does not dispute that platforms use such algorithms; this is shared background.
explanations.D: One-sided — Eriksson calls for legislative regulation; Walcott does not address legislative authority.
explanations.E: Shift in subject — Walcott says users encounter more cross-cutting content online, which implies (E) is true; Eriksson does not deny that any diverse content appears, only that algorithms suppress it relative to provocative content.

difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that the New Deal had economic effects; the disagreement is whether deficit spending was responsible for ending the Depression. A trap answer captures shared acceptance of New Deal spending programs.
stimulus: Ferreira: The New Deal's deficit spending pulled the United States out of the Great Depression by injecting demand into a collapsed economy. Federal employment programs put money in workers' pockets, which they spent on goods and services, generating a multiplier effect that gradually restored economic confidence. Without this fiscal intervention, the Depression would have lasted far longer. Stanton: The New Deal alleviated suffering and reformed financial institutions, but it did not end the Depression — the economy remained deeply depressed through the late 1930s. Full recovery came only with the enormous defense spending triggered by World War II. New Deal deficits were too modest and inconsistent to generate the demand needed for complete recovery.
questionStem: Ferreira and Stanton disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: New Deal programs alleviated economic suffering during the 1930s

choices.label: B
choices.text: World War II military spending boosted the American economy

choices.label: C
choices.text: the federal government ran budget deficits during the New Deal era

choices.label: D
choices.text: New Deal deficit spending was sufficient to end the Great Depression

choices.label: E
choices.text: demand stimulus can in principle restore a depressed economy

explanations.correct: Ferreira argues New Deal deficit spending did pull the economy out of the Depression; Stanton argues it was insufficient and that recovery only came with WWII defense spending. Both directly address and oppose each other on whether New Deal spending was enough to end the Depression.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Stanton explicitly grants that the New Deal alleviated suffering; Ferreira affirms this as well. Neither denies it.
explanations.B: One-sided — Stanton credits WWII spending with full recovery; Ferreira does not address WWII spending at all.
explanations.C: Out of scope — neither speaker disputes the historical fact of deficit spending; Stanton even mentions deficits were 'too modest,' presupposing they occurred.
explanations.E: One-sided — Ferreira implicitly endorses demand stimulus; Stanton's argument concerns the scale of the specific stimulus, not whether demand stimulus can work in principle.

difficultyReason: Both speakers value artistic integrity; they disagree on whether commercial success is compatible with it. A trap answer presents their shared valuation of integrity as a point of disagreement.
stimulus: Inoue: An artist who tailors work to market demands has surrendered the creative independence that makes art meaningful. Commercial success requires producing what audiences already expect, which inevitably narrows the artist's vision and homogenizes culture. The most enduring art has almost always been created in defiance of prevailing tastes, not in service of them. Adjei: Commercial success and artistic integrity are not mutually exclusive. Many artists have reached wide audiences precisely because their genuine vision resonated broadly, not because they compromised it. Financial independence from commercial success can actually free an artist from dependence on institutional patrons, who impose their own constraints on creative work.
questionStem: Inoue and Adjei disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: artistic integrity is a valuable quality in creative work

choices.label: B
choices.text: institutional patronage places constraints on artists' creative freedom

choices.label: C
choices.text: commercial success necessarily compromises an artist's creative integrity

choices.label: D
choices.text: the most enduring artworks have typically been created without regard for market demand

choices.label: E
choices.text: artists should seek to expand the audience for their work

explanations.correct: Inoue argues that tailoring work to the market 'inevitably' narrows vision, implying commercial success necessarily compromises integrity; Adjei directly counters that the two are 'not mutually exclusive.' Both take clear opposing positions on this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers treat artistic integrity as valuable; neither dismisses it.
explanations.B: One-sided — Adjei raises institutional patronage as a constraining force; Inoue does not address patrons at all.
explanations.D: One-sided — Inoue asserts this historical claim; Adjei does not directly contest the historical record, only the general relationship between commerce and integrity.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses whether artists should seek wider audiences as a goal.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that mandatory minimum sentences have costs; disagreement is about whether prosecutorial discretion adequately corrects for their harshness. A trap answer captures their shared critique of rigid sentencing.
stimulus: Okafor: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws produce unjust outcomes by stripping judges of the discretion needed to account for individual circumstances. A first-time, low-level drug offender can face the same prison term as a violent repeat offender. Prosecutors cannot fix this problem — their charging decisions introduce inconsistency without restoring principled case-by-case fairness. Reyes: Mandatory minimums do constrain judges, but prosecutors retain substantial power to calibrate outcomes by choosing which charges to file. In practice, prosecutorial discretion functions as a release valve, allowing the system to avoid the most egregious applications of these laws. The real solution lies in better training prosecutors, not in abolishing mandatory minimums.
questionStem: Okafor and Reyes disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: mandatory minimum sentencing laws limit the discretion available to judges

choices.label: B
choices.text: some mandatory minimum sentences produce outcomes that are disproportionately harsh

choices.label: C
choices.text: prosecutorial discretion adequately compensates for the inflexibility of mandatory minimum laws

choices.label: D
choices.text: violent repeat offenders deserve longer prison sentences than first-time offenders

choices.label: E
choices.text: mandatory minimum laws should be abolished entirely

explanations.correct: Okafor explicitly argues prosecutors cannot fix the harshness of mandatory minimums and that their decisions introduce inconsistency without principled fairness; Reyes explicitly argues prosecutorial discretion functions as an effective 'release valve.' Both take opposing positions on this specific claim.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers accept that mandatory minimums constrain judges; Reyes affirms this while focusing on prosecutorial power as compensation.
explanations.B: Agreement in disguise — Okafor argues minimums are unjust; Reyes grants that 'most egregious applications' must be avoided, implying some outcomes are too harsh.
explanations.D: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses the normative question of what sentences violent offenders deserve.
explanations.E: Shift in subject — Okafor critiques mandatory minimums and implies reform, but does not call for total abolition; Reyes opposes abolition. The disagreement in the stimulus is not about total abolition.

difficultyReason: Both speakers endorse the use of cost-benefit analysis in policy; they diverge on whether it should be the decisive criterion when environmental values are at stake. A trap presents their shared endorsement of cost-benefit analysis as a point of contention.
stimulus: Prasad: Cost-benefit analysis should be the decisive criterion in environmental policymaking. When we quantify the costs of regulation against the economic value of the benefits — cleaner air, reduced health costs, preserved ecosystems — we can make rational, transparent decisions rather than ones driven by emotion or political pressure. Every environmental protection can and should be evaluated on these terms. Delacroix: Cost-benefit analysis is a useful tool, but treating it as decisive in environmental policy is a mistake. Many ecological values — the existence of a species, the integrity of a wilderness — cannot be adequately captured in monetary terms. When cost-benefit calculations exclude or undervalue these things, following them blindly leads to policies that are economically tidy but ethically indefensible.
questionStem: Prasad and Delacroix disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: cost-benefit analysis has any legitimate role in environmental policymaking

choices.label: B
choices.text: environmental regulations impose costs on businesses and the broader economy

choices.label: C
choices.text: the preservation of wild species has value that policymakers should take into account

choices.label: D
choices.text: cost-benefit analysis should serve as the decisive criterion in making environmental policy decisions

choices.label: E
choices.text: some environmental decisions are influenced by political pressure rather than rational analysis

explanations.correct: Prasad argues cost-benefit analysis should be the decisive criterion; Delacroix argues it is a useful tool but must not be treated as decisive because it cannot capture all ecological values. Both take clear, opposing positions on this precise proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Delacroix explicitly calls cost-benefit analysis 'a useful tool,' affirming it has a legitimate role; Prasad obviously endorses it. Neither denies it has any role.
explanations.B: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses the distribution of regulatory costs; Prasad mentions economic value of benefits but not costs imposed on businesses specifically.
explanations.C: Agreement in disguise — Prasad includes 'preserved ecosystems' among benefits and Delacroix argues species existence has value that cost-benefit analysis undervalues. Both treat such value as real; they disagree about whether cost-benefit analysis captures it.
explanations.E: One-sided — Prasad raises political pressure as something rational analysis should replace; Delacroix does not address political pressure at all.
